name: Jū mǎ pāo 車馬包
description: Jū mǎ pāo (Chariot Horse Cannon) is a traditional Chinese matching and trick-taking game that uniquely utilizes the 32 pieces of a Chinese Chess (Xiangqi) set as cards. Played by 3 or 4 players, players treat the chess discs as a deck, shuffling them face-down and forming stacks. It is a game of memory, piece-value calculation, and specific combination-based captures.

history.origins: Dates back to the late Qing dynasty or earlier. The use of Xiangqi pieces as cards is a common practice in Southern China and Southeast Asia (see 'Giog' in Malaysia).
timeline: 1800s: Traditional social game in Southern China.
1900s: Popular among laborers and social clubs in Hong Kong and Guangdong.
Present: Played mostly by enthusiasts and in regional gambling circles.
history.cultural: The name reflects the three most powerful pieces in the game: the Chariot (Ju), Horse (Ma), and Cannon (Pao).
history.evolution: The game evolved from the 'Tam Cuc' family of games but simplified the military hierarchy into a faster, disc-based format.

setup.players: Three or four players. The game is best with three, in which case each receives eight pieces; with four players the 32 Xiangqi pieces are distributed evenly (typically eight per player). No partnerships; each plays for themselves.
setup.deck: A full set of 32 Chinese Chess pieces (16 Red, 16 Black).
setup.dealing: Pieces are shuffled face-down and arranged in 16 stacks of two in a circle. Each player draws a set number of pieces (usually 8).

rules.objective: Win tricks to capture the highest value pieces and score points based on piece rankings.
rules.gameplay:
1. Lead player plays a single piece or combination face-down.
2. Others play the same number of pieces face-down.
3. Reveal all: The highest ranking piece or combination wins the trick and leads next.

strategy.basic: Keep track of which Chariots and Cannons have been played. Because there are only 32 pieces, counting is highly effective.
strategy.intermediate: Pair Management: If you have a Marshal (Red 2) and General (Black 2), they are unbeatable as a pair. Save them for a large 'sweep' of high-value pawns.
strategy.advanced: The 'Hidden Lead': Lead with a low-value Red Soldier to draw out high-value Black Pawns when you suspect an opponent has a weak hand, then use your mid-tier pieces to win later tricks.
tips: Black pieces generally outrank Red counterparts in certain dialects; confirm house rules before playing.
The Black Pawn is surprisingly the most powerful single piece in this scoring variant.
